::: {.bs-editorial-lead}
The Moon can be read as more than an object in the sky. In the Anishinaabe teaching resources used here, **Grandmother Moon** helps mark time through changes in the land, water, plants, animals, weather, and community life.
:::

## Start with the source and the community

Moon teachings are not identical across First Nations. Names, spellings, seasonal timing, and meanings change with language, territory, family, and community. The main teaching sequence on this page comes from a [Matawa Education and Care Centre Science 9 resource](https://matawalearning.ca/application/files/7517/1598/1948/Matawa_Science-Cycles-of-the-Moon.pdf), which identifies its 13 Moons as those of the **Mississaugas of the Credit**. That local connection matters because Port Credit Secondary School stands within the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.

This page is a starting point for learning, not a replacement for an Elder, Knowledge Keeper, language speaker, or community teacher. [*Our Stories: First Peoples in Canada*](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/indigstudies/chapter/13-grandmother-moons/) makes the same point: specific teachings depend on a community's history and culture.

## Grandmother Moon

The local sources use **Grandmother Moon**, rather than Mother Moon. A Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation community notice names her **Tibik Giizis Nookmissmaan** and describes a gathering to honour Grandmother Moon, the movement and cleansing of water, and intentions of gratitude. See page 11 of the [November 2019 *Eaglepress*](https://mncfn.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/November2019FINAL-compressed.pdf).

In these teachings, Grandmother Moon connects observation with relationship and responsibility. Watching the Moon means noticing what is changing around us and considering how people live with those changes.

## The 13 Grandmother Moons

The table below summarizes the Mississaugas of the Credit sequence presented in the [Matawa learning resource](https://matawalearning.ca/application/files/7517/1598/1948/Matawa_Science-Cycles-of-the-Moon.pdf). Gregorian months are approximate guides. A Moon follows a lunar cycle and seasonal signs on the land, not the first and last day of a calendar month.

| Grandmother Moon | Approximate season | Meaning in the cited teaching |
|---|---|---|
| **Mnido Giizis — Spirit Moon** | Most of January | A quiet, reflective time. Some Nations attach significance to the northern lights seen during this Moon. |
| **Makwa Giizis — Bear Moon** | Most of February | A time for reflection. Some teachings connect this Moon with bear cubs being born and reflection on earlier vision quests. |
| **Ziissbaakdoke Giizis — Sugar Moon** | Most of March | Maple sap begins to run and syrup is made. Many Anishinabek communities treat this as the start of a new year. |
| **Namebine Giizis — Sucker Moon** | Most of April | Sucker fish become easier to catch after the lean part of winter. The fish's gift of life supports the people. |
| **Waawaaskone Giizis — Flower Moon** | Most of May | Flowers and medicines begin to grow and bloom. |
| **Odemin Giizis — Strawberry Moon** | Most of June | The heart-shaped strawberry is an important medicine. It carries teachings about healing and reconciliation. |
| **Mskomini Giizis — Raspberry Moon** | Most of July | A time of change, with teachings about family, gentleness, and kindness. |
| **Datkaamin Giizis — Blackberry or Thimbleberry Moon** | July into August | Honours a berry described in the source as producing a large crop about once every three years. |
| **Mdaamiin Giizis — Corn Moon** | Most of August | Teaches the cycle of life and responsibility to future generations. The source connects the rows on a corn cob with generations still to come. |
| **Biinaakwe Giizis — Falling Leaves Moon** | Most of September | Creation makes offerings to Mother Earth through autumn colour and falling leaves. |
| **Mshkawji Giizis — Freezing Moon** | Most of October | A time to prepare for winter and turn toward teachings, songs, and stories. |
| **Mnidoons Giizis Oonhg — Little Spirit Moon** | Most of November | A time for healing, walking a good path, and living well with family and community. |
| **Mnidoons Giizis — Blue Moon / Big Spirit Moon** | Most of December | For some communities, this begins a period of spiritual reflection, purification, and healing. |

The words above should remain connected to their source. Other Anishinaabe communities may use different names, spellings, orders, or teachings because the land and community are different.

## The Moons and the seasons

The names tell what people notice: sap running, fish returning, flowers blooming, berries ripening, corn growing, leaves falling, and water freezing. A Moon is therefore both a way of marking time and a record of relationships with a particular place.

The [Ontario First Nations, Métis, and Inuit Studies curriculum](https://www.edu.gov.on.ca/eng/curriculum/secondary/First-nations-metis-inuit-studies-grades-9-12.pdf) describes the Thirteen Moon Teachings as a yearly calendar followed by many First Nations communities that attends to lunar and natural cycles. The curriculum also notes that the teaching is often represented on a turtle's back.

## Thirteen Moons and 28 days

The 13-Moon teaching presented by Matawa and Centennial College uses **28 days** around the turtle's outer shell. Thirteen groups of 28 days make 364 days, creating a memorable way to think about a seasonal round.

This is a cultural calendar teaching, not a claim that the astronomical Moon always takes exactly 28 days to complete every cycle. NASA explains that the Moon takes about **27.3 days to orbit Earth** and about **29.5 days to go from one New Moon to the next**. See [NASA's answers to common Moon questions](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/top-moon-questions/) and its [Moon phases guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/moon-phases/).

Keeping those ideas distinct lets both forms of knowledge stay clear: the turtle-shell teaching carries relationships, memory, and seasonal meaning, while astronomical measurement describes orbital timing.

## The turtle's back

I have interpreted **“Turtle Rock”** here as **the turtle's back**, sometimes called the turtle-shell calendar. The teaching diagram has 13 larger sections in the centre for the 13 Moons and 28 smaller sections around the edge for the days in the teaching cycle.

This connection is also present in Mississaugas of the Credit community learning. A 2026 *Eaglepress* article describes kindergarten students counting 13 spots on a turtle's back and connecting them to the 13 Moons. See page 14 of [the May 2026 *Eaglepress*](https://mncfn.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/MayEaglepress_2026-Websize.pdf).

The pattern works as a teaching relationship. It should not be turned into a universal anatomy claim that every turtle species or every individual shell must have exactly the same number of visible scutes.

## New Moon and Old Moon

**New Moon** is an astronomical phase. The Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so the side facing Earth receives little direct sunlight and is difficult to see. Afterward, the visible crescent grows, or waxes.

**Old Moon** is an informal sky-watching name for the thin **waning crescent** near the end of a lunar cycle, shortly before New Moon. On this site and in the class announcements, “Old Moon” is used in that observational sense. It is not presented as the name of one of the 13 Grandmother Moons.

NASA lists the phases in order as New Moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, third quarter, and waning crescent. See [NASA's Moon phases guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/moon-phases/).
